newsitem.title: GERMANY: British builder's widow wins German legal fight.
newsitem.headline: British builder's widow wins German legal fight.

text.p: The widow of a British builder who fell to his death on a Leipzig building site in 1994 won a court victory on Wednesday when his former employers were found guilty of negligent manslaughter.
A regional east German court found David Carter and Richard Unterhuber, representing the British and German firms in charge of the building site, both guilty of negligent manslaughter.

Carter, who was also found in breach of safety regulations, was given a suspended jail term of five months and ordered to pay 8,000 marks ($4,630) compensation to Denise Stacey, who has waged a three-year campaign to prosecute her husband's employers.
Unterhuber was ordered to pay a fine of 14,000 marks but received no jail sentence.
Len Stacey, 49, was killed when he fell head first from an eight-metre (26 feet) raised section of a building site in the east German city.
"This result is what we were looking for," George Henderson, a representative of the British Transport and General Workers Union (TGWU), told Reuters after the verdict.

"There is no amount of punishment that can make up for the loss of human life. But that they've been found guilty of negligent manslaughter should be a real deterrent to others. It will be a warning to unscrupulous employers who exploit building workers," he said.
Denise Stacey said the verdict was some comfort, but had hoped both men would be jailed.
Carter said he was sorry and had apologised to the builder's widow hundreds of times.

Judge Petra Wendtland, who tried the case in the town of Eilenburg near Leipzig, said in a telephone interview after the verdict that Stacey's employers should have provided safety barriers on raised levels of the site.
The TGWU, which has supported Denise Stacey's campaign, said some 130 foreign workers died on German building sites in 1996.

German construction trade union IG Bau says a total of nearly 600 workers a year die on sites in the country which often use illegal labour and have been accused of widespread failure to implement safety procedures.
Foreign building firms with lower labour costs, particularly from Britain and Portugal, have been used extensively during the huge reconstruction programme that followed German unification in 1990.
